newsitem.title: KENYA: African summit calls for "neutral force" in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: African summit calls for "neutral force" in Zaire.

text.p: African leaders urged the United Nations Security Council on Tuesday rapidly to deploy a "neutral force" in eastern Zaire to help 1.2 million Hutu refugees facing famine and epidemics.

After a four-hour summit in the Kenyan capital, seven east and central African leaders said the force should create safe corridors to repatriate the refugees to Rwanda and Burundi and provide temporary sanctuary for the huge mass of people.
The leaders called for an immediate ceasefire in fighting between Zaire's ramshackle army and ethnic Tutsi rebels who have captured swathes of eastern Zaire and its main towns.
The rebels declared a unilateral three-week ceasefire on Monday, to allow the refugees safe passage home, but Zaire has not reciprocated.
Zaire boycotted the Nairobi summit, saying it will not attend such talks until foreign troops -- a reference to Rwanda -- have left its territory.
The summit outcome confirmed Africa's refusal to accept sole or even principal responsibility for coping with the continent's worst crisis since the genocide in Rwanda in 1994.
It clearly passed the ball back to the world's powerful nations, the permanent members of the Security Council, and told them to organise a military intervention.
The Council was expected to discuss Zaire later on Tuesday at France's request.

"The summit requested the U.N. Security Council to take urgent measures to ensure the establishment of the safe corridors and temporary sanctuaries by deploying a neutral force," a final communique said.
It said the "sub-region" -- presumably east and central African states -- was ready to contribute. It did not specify that African troops would be offered.

Analysts noted that Rwanda, represented by President Pasteur Bizimungu, agreed the deployment of a military force in eastern Zaire. Only hours earlier Rwanda's foreign minister, Anastase Gasana, said in Brussels his government opposed any such force.

But the analysts noted the key word "neutral". Rwanda's Tutsi army, a central player in the conflict, does not consider France to be neutral and yet Paris has led the running for the deployment of foreign troops to assist the refugees.

The summit said bona fide refugees should be separated from "intimidators", the tens of thousands of former Rwandan government soldiers and Interahamwe militiamen mainly responsible for the genocide against minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus in 1994.
Those armed men fled with civilians abroad, mainly to Zaire, in the weeks after the genocide when they were routed by the mainly Tutsi rebels now in power in Rwanda.
The snag for all who have dealt with the post-genocide crisis in central Africa is that the vast bulk of the Hutu refugees refuse to go home and say they would rather die.
Rwanda's jails already hold more than 80,000 Hutu genocide suspects and many of the refugees have blood on their hands.

With each passing day, less and less is known of the whereabouts and condition of the refugees in Zaire, now without any U.N. protection or support since fighting forced the last international aid workers out of Zaire on Saturday.
The leaders of Kenya, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Uganda, Rwanda, Zambia, Eritrea and the foreign minister of Cameroon attended the Nairobi summit.
"The conflict in eastern Zaire poses a serious threat to the stability of the entire region," Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi said in opening remarks.
An empty seat with a Zairean flag highlighted the absence of Zairean Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, under fire at home for the army's feeble showing against Tutsi rebels.

The political atmosphere in the Zairean capital Kinshasa remained tense on Tuesday and hundreds of Zaireans, defying a ban on anti-Rwanda demonstrations, set up roadblocks and hijacked cars, witnesses said.
Zaire's ailing President Mobutu Sese Seko is in France after three months from home receiving cancer treatment in Europe.
